summary.text: For \(n=2k+1\), the two numbers tested by any matrix entry sum to \(4k+2\); hence if no prime decomposition exists, every entry is zero and so is the determinant, contradicting the assumed nonvanishing when \(k>60\). The remaining cases \(1\le k\le60\) are settled by explicit prime decompositions.

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the integer determinant in the definition of A228623. Thus, with rows and columns indexed by the integers \(i,j\) satisfying \(0\leq i,j<n\), let
\[
 M_n(i,j)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the subtractions are natural-number subtractions, as in the definition of the sequence, and \(a(n)=\det M_n\).

Assume the conjectural hypothesis
\[
 n>120\text{ and }n\text{ odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)\neq 0.
\]
We prove that for every positive integer \(k\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First observe the elementary connection between a nonzero entry of \(M_n\) and a pair of primes symmetric about \(n\). For indices \(0\leq i,j<n\), we have \(j<n\leq n+i\), so \(n+i-j\) involves no truncation: it is the usual nonnegative integer difference. Likewise, \(i<n\leq n+j\), so \(n+j-i\) is also the usual difference. Consequently,
\[
 (n+i-j)+(n+j-i)=2n.
\]
Thus, whenever \(M_n(i,j)=1\), the two numbers
\[
 p=n+i-j,\qquad q=n+j-i
\]
are prime and satisfy \(p+q=2n\).

We will also use the contrapositive form of this observation. If \(2n\) is not a sum of two primes, then there cannot be any indices \(i,j\) for which both \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\) are prime. Hence every entry of \(M_n\) is zero. If \(n\geq1\), this makes \(M_n\) a nonempty zero matrix, whose determinant is zero. Therefore, for every positive \(n\),
\[
 a(n)\neq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2n\text{ is a sum of two primes}.
\]
More explicitly, nonvanishing of the determinant forces at least one matrix entry to be nonzero; since all entries are either zero or one, that entry is one and supplies the two primes just displayed.

Now fix an integer \(k>0\). We split into two cases.

Suppose first that \(k>60\). Set
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd, and
\[
 n=2k+1>2\cdot60+1=121>120.
\]
The assumed nonvanishing conjecture therefore gives \(a(n)\neq0\). By the preceding observation, there are primes \(p,q\) with
\[
 p+q=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
This proves the required conclusion for every \(k>60\).

For completeness, the remaining range \(1\leq k\leq60\) is handled directly. The following table gives, for each such \(k\), a pair of primes \(p,q\). The last column is \(4k+2\), and in every row it equals \(p+q\).
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r@{\qquad}c|r|r|r}
 k&p&q&4k+2&k&p&q&4k+2\\ \hline

27&3&107&110&57&3&227&230\\
28&5&109&114&58&5&229&234\\
29&5&113&118&59&5&233&238\\
30&13&109&122&60&3&239&242
\end{array}
\]
All numbers in the two middle columns are prime. This is immediate for the small primes \(3,5,7,11,13,19\); for the others it can be checked by trial division. Since the largest is \(239\) and \(\sqrt{239}<16\), it suffices to test divisibility by the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), and none of the displayed numbers larger than \(13\) has any such divisor. The equalities in the last column are direct additions. Thus the table proves the desired prime decomposition in every case \(1\leq k\leq60\).

Combining the direct finite range with the determinant argument for \(k>60\), every positive integer \(k\) admits primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
 4k+2=p+q.
\]
Hence the asserted nonvanishing of A228623 for all odd \(n>120\) implies Goldbach's conjecture for all even integers of the form \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\).
